Having gazed [at it], having struck, drawn, and pulled [it], having grasped it and placed the *ādhāra-śakti* in the fire, having caused [the deity] to be present by means of three oblations, [one should place] the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā* below the navel, [extending] from the elements beginning with water up to *prakṛti*, and [the deities] beginning with *tatva-hādi*, ending with *varṇa*, *vāma*, *śiras*, *mantra*, and *amareśa*.

Having observed the impurities of *mala*, *karman*, and *māyā* within the levels from Śrīkaṇṭha down to Bhuvanaśarva, and from [Śarva] and the others up to the station of Vyāpinī, one should strike them, draw them forth, seize them, and place them into the fire; having satiated them with oblations, one should [place] the *vidyā* below the throat—the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *puruṣa* and ending with *māyā*—the phonemes beginning with the Mantras and ending with *gha*, and [the deities] beginning with Vāmā and ending with Aṅguṣṭhamātra.

Having observed the primordial *oṃ* mantra-syllable within the void of the universe, together with impure karma and *māyā*, one should strike it, seize it, and place it within the fire; having gratified it with oblations, [one should contemplate] the *śāntikalā* below the space between the eyebrows, consisting of the syllables *vi-ḍe-śva-ra-sa-dā-śi-va-ga-kha-ka*, the world-realm (*bhuvana*) beginning with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), the Puruṣa-mantra, Vāmā, and ending with Sadāśiva.

"Those whose food is meditation" (dhyānāhārā), and so forth. Having observed the one who possesses the state of the syllable *vyomarūpa*, whose karma is purified of impurity (*malaviśuddhakarma*), together with Mahāmāyā; having struck her, drawn her in, and placed her within the fire; having brought her into proximity—[one observes] from below the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) the Śakti beyond tranquility (*śāntyatītā*), the Śiva-tattva, and so forth, [including] the letters ending in *a* (the vowel *a*), the Īśāna-weapon, the Śiva-mantras beginning with Anivṛtti and ending with Anāśrita, and the world-spheres (*bhuvana*). Having observed the one who possesses the state of the syllable *oṃ*, whose karma is thoroughly purified of impurity along with Mahāmāyā; having struck her, drawn her in, and gathered her, one places her within the fire.

Having brought forth the three bonds (*pāśatraya*)—consisting of impurity (*mala*), action (*karman*), and illusion (*māyā*)—and having visualized them as the cause of the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) and the production of the body of enjoyment (*bhoga-śarīra*) and so forth; and having invoked, worshipped, and offered three oblations (*āhuti*) to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva; [he says]: "In this office of the Lords of Causes (*kāraṇeśa*), I shall initiate this seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*)."

"You must remain in accordance with our will by the command of the Lord. Having thus informed them, he conceives of infinite wombs (*yoni*), worships the Mistress of Speech (*Vāgīśī*) and the Lord of Speech (*Vāgīśa*) who pervade them, completes the rite with three oblations, sprinkles it with the *astra* mantra, strikes it, enters, separates [the soul], and draws it forth.

Having led that [self] to the *dvādaśānta* and gathered it, one should settle it within one's own heart; then, by means of the sequence of abandoning the causal [elements], having led it to the *dvādaśānta*, gathered it, and expelled it, one should contemplate the union of the parents, and [visualize] the self in the form of manifold manifestations within all wombs by means of the *vāmā* arising-seal (*udbhavamudrā*).

Having performed the conjunction simultaneously with the root mantra and having worshipped, one should offer five oblations of *dūrvā* grass; having made the request for the completion of the entire embryo, one should offer fifteen oblations with the root mantra; having made the request for the purpose of birth, one should likewise offer [oblations] and make the request; and for the purpose of [bestowing] authority over all bodies, [one offers] simultaneously.

Having performed [the preliminary rites] twice and having meditated upon the purification of karma that brings about enjoyment within all matrices of the body, one should offer fifteen oblations with the root mantra. Then, having made a formal request regarding the distinctions of place, time, body, and object, [one contemplates] the state of being an enjoyer in various forms, consisting of the experience of pleasure and pain within the self that possesses the subtle body (*liṅgin*).

Having accumulated the *bhoga* and likewise offered it, having informed [the deity] regarding the objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*), and contemplating absorption (*laya*) in the form of supreme delight, one should likewise offer with the root mantra, inform [the deity], and for the purification of the stream of the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*), having offered fifteen oblations with the root mantra and informed [the deity], one enjoys the jewel of karma which is the cause of enjoyment.

For the sake of the cause of generating that [which was previously] obstructed, having offered oblations with the Heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) individually for each [of the rites] such as *nivṛtti* and the rest during purification; and for the purpose of purifying caste, lifespan, experience, latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), and so forth, one should offer fifteen oblations with the Root-mantra (*mūla*)—either joined with the four seed-syllables beginning with the Heart-mantra or used alone.

Having conceived of the separation of pure and impure karma as being of the nature of absolute non-existence, and having offered water with the root mantra, one should request: "O Blessed One, effect the separation of these three bonds of that self, which consist of the impurities of great illusion and karma. Then, [one should perform the rite] seven times with the knife.

Oṃ hmāṃ hvīṃ hrūṃ hyaiṃ hauṃ, [to] Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and Śāntyatīta Kalās; with "haḥ hūṃ phaṭ," having simultaneously severed [the bonds] at that limit using the weapon-mantra (*astra*), having wiped [the area] and made it circular, having placed [the substance] upon a ladle filled with ghee, one should offer it along with clarified butter using that same mantra and then burn it.

Then, in order to eliminate the sprouts of the fetters (*pāśāṅkura*), having offered twenty-five oblations with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having offered forty oblations with the weapon-mantra for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), one should satisfy with oblations the sound, touch, taste, form, and smell, as well as the intellect (*buddhi*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), the mind (*manas*), and the drop (*bindu*), which is white, for the purification of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*).

"O Kāraṇeśa, you must not allow the traveler to reach the state of well-being. O Āṣāḍhaparameśvarī, an obstruction must be established! Having thus informed [the deities] and dismissed them, one should offer fifteen oblations with the *mūla-mantra* for the sake of one's own extraction. Then, having extracted oneself from the Raudrāgni fire, one visualizes oneself as resembling the orb of the autumn moon.

Having brought [the deity] into his own heart, having joined it to the body of the disciple’s thread by means of exhalation (*recaka*), and having worshipped it, he should cast drops of *arghya* water upon the head. Then, for the sake of stabilization, having offered fifteen oblations with the root mantra and having worshipped and satiated the ancestors, he says: "O parents, you two have been exhausted for the sake of the disciple's initiation; therefore, out of compassion, cut this [thread] asunder."

Having informed them, "Go to your own place," and having dismissed them after giving the five full offerings (*pūrṇāpañcaka*), one should [recite] "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śāntyatītā and Śānti," thereby concentrating upon the power of concealment (*tirodhānaśakti*). Then, for the sake of expiation, having offered a hundred or fifty oblations with the root mantra, and having performed a hundred-fold homa with the root mantra for the purification of the power of concealment.

Having visualized the crest-lock (*śikhā*) and the consciousness (*caitanya*) situated at its tip, one should cut the crest-lock with a blade consecrated seven times with the mantra: *oṃ hrūṃ śikhāyai haḥ hūṃ phaṭ*. Having placed it on the tip of a branch encircled with cow dung, and having offered it into the fire with that same mantra, one should burn it. Once purified by this process, it shall transcend [its former state] and attain the nature of Śiva. Thus.

Having first offered himself as before and brought [the deity] into his own heart, he should perform the meditation on the state of equal flavor (*samarasībhāvanā*). Then, taking the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*) and spoon (*sruva*) together with clarified butter by means of the conch-like mudrā, and rising up while recollecting Śiva who pervades all levels of existence (*adhvan*), he should—by means of the unity of the disciple’s self, vital breath, and mind—recollect that consciousness within the *suṣumnā* as the flow of the primordial sound (*nāda*).

Having visualized [the Self] as resembling a pure crystal gem, reciting the mantra according to the path taught by the Guru, and gradually abandoning these causal factors, one should—while remembering that the powers have dissolved at the limit and emitting a stream like clarified butter—unite [the Self] with Śiva, who is beyond the seventh [cakra], transcendent, at the end of the twelve [fingers], beyond the mind, and devoid of objective existence.

Then, having bestowed the six qualities upon [the deceased] with three oblations of clarified butter—reciting *oṃ hāṃ ātman sarvajño bhava svāhā*—and having united him with the fire situated on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should dismiss Śiva and cremate the corpse with its head to the south, according to the rule beginning with those words. Because of the statement that one may take up the levels beginning with Nivṛtti either simultaneously or sequentially, the simultaneous application is concluded here.
This concludes the *Kṣiptāntyeṣṭi*.
Then, having bathed, the performer, being pure, should recite the eleven-fold [mantra] for as long as is appropriate for non-meditation; he should perform the ritual action according to the rules.

Then, having first purified the self and so forth up to the junction of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*), and having returned after performing the deposition on the paths (*adhvan-nyāsa*), he should look down from here to below the knees while reciting "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the *nivṛtti*-kalā," which contains the principles (*tattva*) and so forth, using the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

Having struck [the disciple] and taken [the consciousness], one should place it ending with *namaḥ* in the fire. In this way, having visualized the *vidyā* of *pratiṣṭhā*, *śānti*, and *śāntyatītā* within the *nābhi*, throat, between the eyebrows, and the *brahmarandhra*—with their respective internal essences (*tatvāntagarbha*)—one should strike them and place them in the fire.

Having sprinkled the disciple on the heart with the *astra-mantra*, one should strike him right there with a flower using the *nārācamudrā*, saying "Oṃ haḥ huṃ phaṭ. Then, having emitted that heart [of the disciple] by means of one's own *recaka* breath and entered it by means of the *pūraka* breath, one should contemplate the consciousness (*caitanya*) situated within the seed-syllable *haṃsa*.

Having severed [the bonds] with "oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ huṃ phaṭ," having separated [the soul] by means of the *jyeṣṭhā* [mudrā], and having drawn it forth with the *aṅkuśa* (goad) mudrā ending in *svāhā*, one should contemplate the *jīva*—which has the form of a drop on the tip of a blade of grass—having led it to the *dvādaśānta* while recollecting the root mantra, and [then unite it] with the *ātma-mantra* ending in *namaḥ*.

Having gathered [the breath] with the *saṃhāramudrā*, having expelled it through the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*), and having established it within one’s own heart by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), one should perform retention (*kumbhaka*). Then, recollecting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) and employing the *udbhavamudrā* with one’s own mantra, one should lead [the breath] to the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*) by means of the sequential abandonment of the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, and having gathered it there, [one should proceed].

Having brought [the breath] to the middle of the eyebrows by means of the *sṛṣṭi* [breath], and having expelled it through the *recaka* [exhalation] into the fire, one should simultaneously unite it with the *kalās*. Having contemplated the cessation of obstructions, and having offered a hundred oblations for each *kalā* with the root mantra, and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*, [one says]: "O Great Goddess, by your will, this reversal of the sequence has been performed by me."

"By your will, O Lord of the World, let him not be obstructed by the Triṇoman [impurity]. By your will, may this purified one attain the state of Śiva through the transcendence of [the stages]. Having thus prayed for the welfare [of the disciple], and for the sake of purification, he extracts the disciple’s self—which is the obstacle—from the fire of Raudrī by means of the *saṃhāriṇī* [mantra] of his own self-mantra.

Having brought one’s own heart, which resembles the orb of the autumn moon, [into the mouth] by means of the inhalation (*pūraka*) through the left [nostril], and having made it of a single flavor (*samarasībhāva*), one should join it with Śiva as before using the conch-like mudrā. Having sat down and assumed the six qualities as before, one should perform the remaining rites as previously described. Briefly, in due order, this is the funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*) for one initiated into Nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the "Brief Ritual for the Funeral Rite" in the *Kriyākramadyotikā* composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya.
Homage to the illustrious Vallidevasenī!

Hari Om. Om. In the year [blank], during the month of Tai, on the first day—beginning from that first day and continuing for ten days—having specially worshipped Śiva every single day with a focused mind.

Having gratified him with each one of the mantras of the *sadyojāta*, *vāmadeva*, *aghora*, *tatpuruṣa*, and *īśāna* [faces], as well as the *hṛdaya*, *śiras*, *śikhā*, *kavaca*, and *astra* mantras—each joined with the name of the initiation and ending in *svāhā*—and having worshipped him with [mantras] ending in *namaḥ*, fed him, and offered the *piṇḍa* ending in *svadhā*, one should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one’s capacity. [Salutation] to the venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti. Now, on the first or third day, one should collect the bones. As stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
On the third or the fourth day, while reciting the Astra-mantra, [he should perform the rite];
or else—on the first, third, fifth, or even the seventh day—the twice-born should not perform the collection of bones (*asthisañcayana*).

In that case, if there is a pacification of the form of the cremation fire, he should produce the Śiva-fire near the funeral pyre and offer a hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra for the sake of expiation.
Preceded by worship, one should offer three oblations for each of the principles beginning with earth:

(l. 10) *oṃ hāṃ* to the earth principle, obeisance; *oṃ hāṃ* to the water principle, obeisance; to the fire principle, obeisance; to the air principle, obeisance; (l. 11) to the space principle, obeisance; to the smell principle, obeisance; to the taste principle, obeisance.

Homage to the reality of form (*rūpa-tattva*). Homage to the reality of touch (*sparśa-tattva*). (l. 12) Homage to the reality of sound (*śabda-tattva*). Homage to the reality of the generative organ (*upastha-tattva*). Homage to the reality of the anus (*pāyu-tattva*). Homage to the reality of the feet (*pāda-tattva*). Homage to the reality of the hands (*pāṇi-tattva*). (p. 69a, l. 1) Homage to the reality of speech (*vāk-tattva*). Homage to the reality of the nose (*nāsā-tattva*). Homage to the reality of the tongue (*jihvā-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the reality of the eye (*cakṣus-tattva*). Homage to the reality of the skin (*tvak-tattva*). (l. 2)

Salutation to the principle of hearing (*śrotra-tattva*). Salutation to the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*). Salutation to the principle of ego (*ahaṃkāra-tattva*). Salutation to the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*). (l. 3) Salutation to the principle of the qualities (*guṇa-tattva*).

Salutation to the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*). Salutation to the principle of the person (*puruṣa-tattva*). Salutation to the principle of passion (*rāga-tattva*). Salutation to the principle of necessity (*niyati-tattva*). (l.

4) Salutation to the principle of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*). Salutation to the principle of limited agency (*kalā-tattva*). Salutation to the principle of time (*kāla-tattva*). Salutation to the principle of illusion (*māyā-tattva*).

Having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Śuddhavidyā," "obeisance to the principle of Īśvara," "obeisance to the principle of Sadāśiva," "obeisance to the principle of Śakti," and "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Śiva," and having offered three oblations for each ending in svāhā,

one should then extract [the remains] using the mantras of Sadyojāta and the others for the feet, private parts, heart, mouth, and head, and cast them into the milk upon the blade of the razor placed on the triple wooden stand.

Then, one should place [the vessel] in a pure location. One should cast it into the water of a sacred ford (tīrtha) that has been sealed with earth. One should cast the ashes into the water with verses.

"Salutation to Śrī Puṇyakoṭīśvara. One should offer [this] on a riverbank or at the edge of a pond; or else, having prepared cakes by hand and having decorated a pavilion with canopies and the like, one should construct a two-cubit altar in the middle of the pavilion.
To the east of that, having prepared a square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with a single rim and having smeared it with cow dung,
one should place a heap of rice, grain, sesame, black gram (*māṣa*), mung bean (*mudga*), and other grains in the center. Having drawn a lotus in its middle,

one should arrange four jars in the compartments starting from the northeast (*īśāna*), four jars in the western compartment, the jar of Śiva (*śivakumbha*) in the center, and [two jars] on the southern and northern sides.

Having thus established eleven jars one by one, and having adorned them with cloth, golden lotuses, coconut fruits, mango sprouts, and so forth; immediately thereafter, having washed the vessel for the *arghya* for the guru’s bath and the *sakalīkaraṇa* with the *astra-mantra*, and having prepared the ordinary *arghya*; having performed the worship of the gateway (*dvārapūjā*) as in the daily rite, and having carried out the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the internal sacrifice (*antaryajana*), and the purification of the substances and mantras for the special *arghya*; and having prepared the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), [he prepares] the *pañcagavya-arghya*.

Having sprinkled the sacrificial hall with water and the *astra* [mantra], and having scattered the *vikira* offerings consecrated with the *astra* mantra, one should adorn [the site] with a deer-skin, a cloth, a crown, and so forth. Having worshipped the ten weapons starting from the northeast and ending in the east, one should [worship] in the central jar: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti; obeisance to Anantāsana; obeisance to Ananta."

In the corners of the northeast and southeast: *namaḥ aiśvaryāya* (homage to Sovereignty); *namaḥ vairāgyāya* (homage to Dispassion); *namaḥ jñānāya* (homage to Knowledge); *namaḥ dharmāya* (homage to Dharma).

In the directions from the north to the east: *namaḥ anaiśvaryāya* (homage to Non-sovereignty); *namaḥ avairāgyāya* (homage to Non-dispassion); *namaḥ ajñānāya* (homage to Ignorance); *namaḥ adharmāya* (homage to Non-dharma).
Between the southwest and the northeast: *namaḥ adhaśchadanāya* (homage to the lower covering); *namaḥ ūrdhvacchadanāya* (homage to the upper covering).

In the center: *namaḥ* to the lotus; *namaḥ* to the seeds; *namaḥ* to the pericarp; (l. 6) *namaḥ* to the filaments; *namaḥ* to the petals; *namaḥ* to the stalk; *namaḥ* to the sprout; (l. 7) *namaḥ* to the bulb.
In the northeast of the pericarp: *namaḥ* to Manonmanī. (l. 8)
In the filaments beginning with Īśāna and ending with the East: Salutation to Sarvabhūtadamanī. Salutation to Balapramathinī.
Salutation to Balavikaraṇī. Salutation to Kalavikaraṇī. Salutation to Kālī. Salutation to Raudrī. Salutation to Jyeṣṭhā. Salutation to Vāmā.
In the center of the pericarp: *namaḥ śaktimaṇḍalāya*.
To the Lord (*īśvara*), the sovereign of the power-circle (*śaktimaṇḍala*): *namaḥ*.
On the circle at the tip of the pericarp: *namaḥ vanhimaṇḍalāya*.
Homage to Rudra, the lord of the fire-maṇḍala.
On the circle at the tips of the filaments: homage to the moon-maṇḍala;
homage to Viṣṇu, the lord of the moon-maṇḍala.
On the circumference at the tip of the petals: *namaḥ sūryamaṇḍalāya* (homage to the solar disc).
*namaḥ sūryamaṇḍalādhipataye brahmaṇe* (homage to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc).
*namaḥ śivāsanāya* (homage to the seat of Śiva). Above that, *namaḥ śivamūrttaye* (homage to the form of Śiva).
Having performed the placement of the mantras of Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna from the feet to the head—
one who resembles pure crystal, has three eyes, bears the moon upon his crest,
possesses the Vyākhyā-mudrā, is endowed with the fire of knowledge, holds a trident in hand, and has four arms— (one should meditate on him).
Having meditated thus: "Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with serpent-earrings," [one should say]:

"Obeisance to the body of knowledge (vidyādeha). [One should offer] obeisance to the faces beginning with Sadyojāta and to the eyes. Having invoked Śiva by means of the root mantra and worshipped him with the services beginning with installation (sthāpana), [one should proceed].
O Lord, Sovereign of all the worlds, remain present within this vessel with a spirit of affection until the conclusion of the worship.

Having thus informed [the deity], and having offered a welcome and water for the feet (*arghya*), one should assign the heart-mantra and the other mantras to the locations starting from the heart and ending with the hands. Having established oneness with the root mantra, protected with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and encased by circling counter-clockwise with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), one should offer the *mṛta-mudrā*.

Then, having rendered [the deity] supreme with the great mudrā using the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and having bound the five-faced mudrā, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the *arghya* offering.

With the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should offer *dūrvā* grass, flowers, unbroken rice, and so forth. Having visualized the limbs of the ritual bath—such as anointing with oil, rubbing with unguents, and immersion—one should bathe [the deity] with drops of *arghya* water. Having mentally and with devotion offered sandalwood paste, unbroken rice, *dūrvā* grass, a golden loincloth, a girdle, a sacred thread, earrings, ornaments, and various garments, and having worshipped with three handfuls of flowers, one should display the *manoratha-mudrā*. Then, having worshipped the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*) with the *Sadyojāta* and other mantras, one should worship the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*).

In the west, obeisance to the form Sadyojāta. In the north, obeisance to the secret Vāmadeva. (p. 71b, l. 1) In the south, obeisance to the heart Aghora. In the east, obeisance to the face Tatpuruṣa. (l. 2) Obeisance to the head Īśāna. To the eyes of Īśāna in the north—obeisance. In the southeast, obeisance to the heart. (l. 3) To the head of Netra in the north—obeisance.

In the southwest: *namaḥ śikhāyai*. In the northwest: *namaḥ kavacāya*. Having worshipped and offered the *arghya* to the weapon (*astra*) in the directions starting from the north and ending with the east, one should display the *sṛṇi*, *makara*, *triśūla*, *padma*, and *dhenu* mudrās for the [five] Brahmans, and the *namaskāra* mudrā for the limbs (*aṅga*). Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) and having displayed the *mahāmudrā*, one should contemplate the oneness of all [deities] with Śiva.

Then, in the second enclosure, in the directions starting from Īśāna and ending with the East: *namaḥ* to Śikhaṇḍin; *namaḥ* to Śrīkaṇṭha; *namaḥ* to Trimūrti; *namaḥ* to Ekarudra; *namaḥ* to Ekanetra; *namaḥ* to Śivottama; *namaḥ* to Sūkṣma; *namaḥ* to Ananta. In the third enclosure:
Homage to Caṇḍa. Homage to Devī. Homage to Skanda. Homage to Vṛṣabha. Homage to Vināyaka. (p. 72a, l. 1) Homage to Bhṛṅgin. Homage to Mahākāla. Homage to Nandin.
[In] the fourth enclosure.

Salutation to Īśāna. Salutation to Kubera. Salutation to Vāyu. Salutation to Varuṇa. Salutation to Nirṛti. Salutation to Yama. Salutation to Agni. Salutation to Indra. Salutation to Viṣṇu. Salutation to Brahmā.

In the fifth enclosure: obeisance to the trident; obeisance to the mace; obeisance to the goad; obeisance to the noose; obeisance to the sword; obeisance to the staff; obeisance to the spear; obeisance to the thunderbolt; obeisance to the discus.
Having worshipped with "Salutation to Padma," [one should meditate on the deity] who has a blue throat and three eyes, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
and holding a trident, a skull-cup, and a sword in his right hands, while displaying the gesture of fearlessness.
In his left hands he holds a serpent, an axe, a staff, and the gesture of granting boons;
he has four faces and eight arms, resplendent with a white complexion,
adorned with all ornaments, and decorated with snake-earrings.

Having meditated thus and having worshipped with all the ritual services beginning with the invocation, one should thereafter worship the eleven Rudras, from Īśāna to Śānānta, individually according to the sequence of invocation and so forth, preceded by the sixfold rising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) and using the mantras for the seat, the form, and the root mantra.
As follows: In the central jar: "Homage to the seat of Mahādeva; homage to the form of Mahādeva.
[One should worship] Mahādeva as four-armed and three-eyed, white in color, holding the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and an axe in his right hands, and the best of deer in his left hands.
Salutation to Mahādeva.
(Jya) In the northeast pitcher:
salutation to the seat of Kapālīśa; salutation to the form of Kapālīśa.

Kapālīśa has four arms and is white as a conch shell; he possesses four hands, is endowed with yellow garments and other ornaments, and holds a trident along with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Salutation to Kapālīśa. (Jya) (l.
5) Salutation to the one seated upon Bhavodbhava. Salutation to the form of Bhavodbhava.
And [salutation] to the three-eyed Bhavodbhava, adorned with matted hair and the crescent moon. (l. 6)
Resembling crystal, with four arms, holding a sword, a shield, and displaying the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness—homage to Bhavodbhava!
Homage to the one who is the seat of the God of Gods! Homage to the embodiment of the God of Gods!
The god of gods, four-armed, with a form white as cow’s milk, adorned with all ornaments, [holding] fire and Kṛṣṇa, and granting boons and fearlessness. Homage to the god of gods. (Jya)

Salutation to Bhīmāsana; salutation to Bhīmamūrti. One should meditate upon Bhīma as four-armed, three-eyed, and white in appearance, holding a sword, the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), along with a trident, and adorned with a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmakuṭa*).
Salutation to Bhīma. (Jya) (l.
2) Salutation to the one whose seat is victory. Salutation to the one whose form is victory.
Victory is white in appearance, with a radiance equal to ten million suns. (l. 3)
Four-armed and three-eyed, he holds a fire, an axe, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Salutation to Vijaya. (Jya) (l.
4) Salutation to the seat of Īśāna. Salutation to the form of Īśāna.
[I salute] Īśāna, who has the luster of crystal and is adorned with pearls and other ornaments. (l. 5)
To the three-eyed, four-armed deity who holds a trident, fire, and the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness:
salutation to Īśāna.
Salutation to the one seated upon Nīlalohita. Salutation to the embodiment of Nīlalohita.

One should meditate on the form of Nīlalohita, adorned with white garments and other ornaments, possessing four arms, holding a deer and a chisel, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Homage to Nīlalohita. (Jya) (l.
9) Homage to the seat of Śaṅkara. Homage to the form of Śaṅkara.
[One should meditate on] Śaṅkara as having the luster of a white color, with three eyes and four arms. (l. 10)
Adorned with divine garments, [he holds] a black axe and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Salutation to Śaṅkara. (Jya) (l. 11) Salutation to the one whose seat is Rudra. Salutation to the form of Rudra.
[He is] Rudra, three-eyed, red-hued, holding a trident and a black [object], and granting boons and fearlessness. (p. 73b, l. 1)
One should meditate upon her as having four arms, adorned with all ornaments.
Salutation to Rudra.
(Jya) Salutation to the seat of Śiva. Salutation to the form of Śiva.
Śiva has three eyes, is white in luster, and is adorned with a crown of matted hair.
One should meditate on Kṛṣṇa seated in a comfortable posture, holding the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) and an axe (paraśu), and bestowing boons (vara).

Salutations to Śiva. (Jya) Having worshipped [the deity] individually with all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*) beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*), and having subsequently performed the rites ending with the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the kindling (*dīpana*) according to the procedure prescribed for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), one should worship Rudra in the midst of the fire and offer a hundred oblations (*homa*) with the *brahmamantras* beginning with Sadyojāta.

One should offer oblations of fuel-sticks (*samid*), clarified butter (*ājya*), grains, and parched rice (*lāja*). Having performed one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra and having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should present the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, lamps, and so forth.

Thereafter—having placed *darbha* grass upon a plantain leaf and having worshipped Mahādeva and the other deities with perfumes, flowers, and so on—one should present the sacrificial offering (*bali*) ending with "svāhā. Then, having prepared nine squares to its east: "Obeisance to Rudra beginning with Īśāna, to Raudra, to Kṣetrapāla, and to the Piśācas. In the central square:

One should worship those Kṣetrapālas who dwell in fierce places and perform fierce deeds like Rudra, as well as others who have attained the state of Piśācas; having entreated them with the words "Release [him]," one should cast down the offering of food (*balipuṣṭi*). To the Bhūtas and Grahas, [one says] "Homage to Kuśmāṇḍa. Having given the *bali* to Kuśmāṇḍa...

Having gratified the Brahmins with gifts, and having offered oblations three times each with the mantras ending in *svāhā* up to the end of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and having offered a hundred oblations with the *astra* and *aghora* mantras for the sake of expiation, and having given the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should unite oneself with the state of Rudra. Having united that [self] situated on the mound with the fire situated within, [one should proceed].

Having offered the *bali* to Brahmā and the other deities, having dismissed the fire, and having performed the *bali* rite, one should dismiss that [offering]. Having satisfied those whose wealth is austerity (*tapodhana*) with food and other provisions, and having satisfied eight observers of the Great Vow (*mahāvrata*) or Pāśupatas and others with garments and sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the ritual procedure for the *rudrabali* is completed. Salutation to Vikaṭacakra-Vināyaka. On the first day, every day, every third day, every fifth day, every seventh day, or every ninth day, having established a water-pot (*kumbha*), one should install a stone. A stone [image] must be prepared for the preceptor (*ācārya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and the sons [of the preceptor].

For Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others, it should be constructed with bricks. It should have a width of three finger-breadths and a height of five finger-breadths. Then, the wise one should draw a square endowed with all the proper characteristics. Having drawn the figure of a man [with the mantra]: "Oṃ sauṃ, obeisance to the state of being a spirit (bhūtatva)."

The best of teachers should avoid [a site] that is of discordant dimensions, has cavities, is split or cracked, is sunken, has a difficult pillar, or is ancient. Having placed a jar filled with a *droṇa* measure [of grain], and having offered incense and lamps encircled by thread—the characteristics of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) have been declared... that door should be constructed.

Having adorned [the site] with red garments and the like, as well as plantains, coconuts, and so forth, one should prepare a secondary altar (*upavedi*) in the center, measuring one cubit in width, eight finger-breadths in height, square and like the surface of a mirror, with a depth of four finger-breadths below and two cubits in length.

Having dug out a circular shape to the east and west of that, eighteen finger-breadths in circumference, and having performed the reverse placement (*viparītanyāsa*), one digs the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) while reciting: *Oṃ pitāmahe astrāya phaṭ*. Then, one purifies the vessel for the guest-offering (*arghyapātra*) with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).

To the father and grandfather, *astrāya hūṃ phaṭ*. Having worshipped [the vessel] seven times and consecrated it with mantras, having protected and veiled it, having shown the *dhenumudrā*, and having scattered white flowers, having sprinkled the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) with the *astra-mantra*, and having drawn a lotus upon which the seven grains are placed, having strewn *darbha* grass and flowers around it, and having offered a seat in its center with the words "Salutation to Mahādeva’s army," one should install the image (*mūrti*).

*Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahādeva.* Having thus invoked [the deity], and having displayed the *sthāpana*, *sannidhāna*, *sannirodhana*, and *dhenu-mudrās*, immediately thereafter, in the pitchers beginning with the northeast (*īśāna*), [one should offer salutations]: Salutation to Kapālīśa; salutation to Bhavodbhava; salutation to Devadeva; salutation to Bhīma; salutation to Vijaya; salutation to Īśāna; salutation to Nīlalohita; salutation to Śaṅkara; salutation to Rudra; salutation to Śiva. (jya)

"Salutation to Sadyojāta; salutation to Pramardana. Having worshipped thus, and having offered incense, lamps, water for rinsing the mouth, and the *arghya* offering, immediately thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras beginning with the Heart. One should worship with "Salutation to the Heart" on the southeast petal; "Salutation to the Head" on the northeast petal; "Salutation to the Crest" on the southwest petal; "Salutation to the Armor" on the northwest petal; "Salutation to the Eyes" in front of the deity; and "Salutation to the Weapon" in the directions starting from the north and ending with the east. [Then] the food offering (*naivedya*).

Having performed the worship ending with incense, lamps, betel, and *japa*, and having requested, "One should place [the stone] upon the rock," he should summon the disciple. Having given him ashes, a garment, a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and so forth, and having placed the garment over his left shoulder, [the preceptor], standing facing east, takes the stone in his right hand and says:

"To all the ancestors, *arghya* svāhā! With the auspicious sound of a conch, [he performs] the oil-anointing... [with the mantra] "For the armor of the ancestors against anthill-earth and so forth, *huṃ phaṭ*. Having thus bathed and adorned [himself] with new garments and other ornaments.

Having established [the offering] with the words, "To the ancestors and to Skanda, svāhā," and having offered incense and lamps, one should present parched grain, cakes, coconut fruit, and so forth, saying, "To all the ancestors, svāhā. Having given the food offering (*naivedya*), drinking water, betel, incense, lamps, and the like, and having caused a great sound with various musical instruments, one should fold a cloth three times over and place it in the middle [of the vessel] together with sesame seeds, *darbha* grass, and flowers. "Obeisance to the earth element (*pṛthvī-tattva*). Obeisance to the water element (*ap-tattva*). Obeisance to the fire element (*tejas-tattva*). Obeisance to the wind element (*vāyu-tattva*). Obeisance to the space element (*ākāśa-tattva*)."

Homage to the principle of hearing. Homage to the principle of touch. Homage to the principle of sight. Homage to the principle of the tongue. Homage to the principle of smell. (l. 7) Homage to all mantras. Homage to all gods. (l. 8) Homage to all ṛṣis. Homage to all beings. Homage to all ancestors. (l. 9) Having thus performed the libation, [one should proceed].

In the eastern pit, [one should offer] together with sesame, *darbha* grass, and cotton: "Obeisance to the principle of sound (*śabda-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of touch (*sparśa-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of form (*rūpa-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of taste (*rasa-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of smell (*gandha-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of speech (*vāk-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of the feet (*pāda-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of the anus (*pāyu-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of the generative organ (*upastha-tattva*); obeisance to the father Īśāna; obeisance to the grandfather Sadāśiva; obeisance to the great-grandfather Śānta. Having thus offered libations with the words "Obeisance to the ancestors," [one proceeds] to the western pit.

[Offerings] accompanied by sesame, *darbha* grass, and cotton. Homage to the principle of speech (*vacana-tattva*). Homage to the principle of movement (*gamana-tattva*). (l. 5) Homage to the principle of giving (*dāna-tattva*). Homage to the principle of emission (*visarga-tattva*). Homage to the principle of bliss (*ānanda-tattva*). Homage to the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*). (l. 6) Homage to the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*). Homage to the principle of ego (*ahaṃkāra-tattva*). Homage to the principle of consciousness (*citta-tattva*). (l. 7) Homage to the grandfathers (*pitāmaha*). Homage to all the ancestors (*pitṛ*). Homage to the perfected ones (*siddha*). Homage to the mothers (*mātṛ*). (l. 8) Homage to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*)—having thus performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*).

Thereafter, in the central pit: *namaḥ* to the principle of Time (*kālatattva*), *namaḥ* to the principle of Necessity (*niyatitattva*), *namaḥ* to the principle of Knowledge (*vidyātattva*), *namaḥ* to the principle of Attachment (*rāgatattva*), *namaḥ* to the principle of the Person (*puruṣatattva*), *namaḥ* to the principle of Illusion (*māyātattva*). Having thus offered libations with the words *namaḥ* to the Skandas and the Fathers (*pitṛs*), [he proceeds] to the eastern pit with sesame, *darbha* grass, and cotton: *namaḥ* to the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyātattva*), *namaḥ* to the principle of the Lord (*īśvaratattva*), *namaḥ* to Caṇḍa and the Grandfathers (*pitāmahas*). Having thus offered libations in three ways, [the rite is completed].

Thereafter—in the western trench—having offered libations three times with sesame, *darbha* grass, and cotton, saying: "Obeisance to the Principle called Sadāśiva; obeisance to the Principle of Śakti; obeisance to the Principle of Śiva; obeisance to the Lord of Gaṇas; obeisance to the Grandfathers.
Then, in the central trench—having offered libations three times, saying: "Svāhā to Skanda; svāhā to Caṇḍa; svāhā to the Lord of Gaṇas."

Thereafter—in the eastern pit—having offered libations accompanied by sesame, *darbha* grass, and cotton, saying: "Obeisance to the ancestors (*pitṛbhyo namaḥ*); obeisance to the mothers (*mātṛbhyo namaḥ*); obeisance to Skanda (*skandāya namaḥ*).

Thereafter—in the western pit—[having offered libations] accompanied by sesame, *darbha* grass, and cotton, [saying]: "Obeisance to the mothers (*mātṛbhyo namaḥ*); obeisance to the gods (*devebhyo namaḥ*); obeisance to the sages (*ṛṣibhyo namaḥ*)."
Homage to the elements. (l. 8) Homage to the hosts. Having offered libations, [he places] that which is accompanied by sesame, *darbha* grass, and cotton into the central pit.
(l. 9) Homage to the ancestors. Homage to Caṇḍa. Svāhā to Sadyojāta. Svāhā to Vāmadeva. (l. 10) Svāhā to Aghora.
Svāhā to Tatpuruṣa. Svāhā to Īśāna. (l. 11) Svāhā to the Weapon (*astra*). Svāhā to the Eyes. Svāhā to the Armor (*kavaca*).
*Śikhāyai svāhā*. *Śirase svāhā*. *Hṛdayāya svāhā*. *Pitṛbhyaḥ svāhā*. *Caṇḍāya svāhā*—having thus offered libations (*tarpaṇa*).

Having daily fed the Brahmins, having performed the worship of Maheśvara, and having first offered the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) for ten days and so forth, having presented various offerings such as rice and molasses.

Having offered incense and lamps, and having subsequently placed the stone upon the jars, one should circumambulate the temple of Śiva accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments. Then, on the northern bank of the river, one should deposit the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), the jars, the stone, and the other items behind the opening of the banner.

Thereafter, having performed the water-libation with the formula "Svadhā, obeisance to Skanda, Caṇḍa, the Lord of the Gaṇas, and the ancestors," and having performed the worship of the preceptor and the worship of the Brāhmaṇas, the ritual procedure for the stone is completed.
Now follows the procedure for the Ekoddiṣṭa rite.

Regarding the impurity (*āśauca*) beginning from the eleventh day: on the first day, after the purification of the house, one should perform the following on the preceding evening. Having seated [the deity] upon a western-facing seat—[the deity] whose characteristics have been described as *kamalā* by the teacher—one should grasp the hand, which is like a sprout, with the hand that is likewise [prepared]. Having addressed [the deity] with the *Saṃpriyaṅgirā* mantra and having offered the oblation (*upahāra*), an invitation (*kṣaṇa*) must be made for the auspicious Śiva-śrāddha for the sake of the pure-faced Śiva.

Having thus petitioned, he should grant permission, saying, "So be it. During that night, recollecting the Supreme Lord and restraining the desires of the senses, he should sleep. On the following day, having performed his bath and daily obligatory rites, he should remain without food. In the afternoon, having performed his bath and daily obligatory rites, he should honor him [the teacher] who has arrived with a seat, a place to sit, and other such offerings.

Having smeared the courtyard for the planetary deities with cow dung, and having drawn two circular maṇḍalas extending from east to west and north to south, the practitioner, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), performs the reverse placement of the hands. Having scattered kuśa grass with tips pointing southward and sesame seeds within these two maṇḍalas as part of the general *arghya* offering, he worships the southern maṇḍala with a white flower while reciting the *astra-mantra*.

There, for the washing of the feet... having worshipped with the heart-mantra and offered the *arghya* in the northern [mandala], and having seated the invited [deity] in the southern mandala; when the initiation-name is not joined with sesame seeds as the occasion requires, one should offer the *arghya* with one's own *dvādaśānta*. Having washed the feet with clay using the initiation-name preceded by the seed-syllable of Vāmadeva, and having sipped water (*ācamana*) in the northern mandala, one should enter within.

Having himself entered [the inner sanctum], at a pure seat or similar location, facing either west or north, he should instruct [the disciple] with his left hand. Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in reverse, he should wash the *arghya* vessel with the *astra-mantra*. Filling it with pure water from [a vessel held] on his head, he should cast sesame seeds into it. With the *sadyojāta-mantra*, he should place a purifying blade of grass (*pavitra*) accompanied by perfume, *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) into it using the *śikhā-mantra*.

Having consecrated [the water] with the *hṛdaya*[-mantra] and protected it, having sprinkled the ritual substances (*dravya*) with that water, one should consecrate the fragrance with the *hṛdaya*, the flower with the *śiras*, the incense and lamp with the *śikhā*, and the garment, sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and so forth, with the *kavaca*. Having remembered [the deity] and made this request, and being told by him, "Do so," [one should perform the rite] with *darbha* grass... having given [the water] to him with the *sadyojāta* [-mantra] while keeping the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).

"I invoke... [and] shall supplicate. Having performed the triad beginning with invocation and installation by means of the left [hand], using the name joined with the root mantra and the desired [deity's name] in the dative case and accompanied by *namas*, and having performed the protection (*rakṣā*) with sesame seeds in an anti-clockwise direction starting from the northeast (*īśāna*), [he offers] the *arghya* for the presence [of the deity] with flowers, *kuśa* grass, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), while kneeling on the ground in the northeast.

Having ascended sequentially from the crown of the head (*mūrdhan*) down to the feet, one should offer perfume and flowers with the *vāma* [mantra], incense and a lamp with the *āra* [mantra], and the purifier (*pavitra*) with the *īśāna* [mantra]. One should say, "May it be complete" (*sampūrṇam astu*), and [the other] should reply, "May it be well; may it be complete. Then, having placed that [purifier] along with the *pavitra* into his hand...

Taking some of that water in a certain leaf, one should place the arghya-vessel at the southwest (nairṛtyāṃ), which is the station of the ancestors (pitṛsthāna). Having prepared it on pure ground for the purpose of eating and cleansing, and having set it aside, one should take the other offerings and [place them] in the general arghya-water.

Having sprinkled [the area] with water, having placed before him a vessel made of gold or other materials—or a leaf of the *kadalī* tree or similar—according to his ability, starting from the east; having given water for washing the hands and purified them; having offered various foods including ghee, molasses, sesame, and side dishes; and having first cast the *japa* into that [vessel], he consecrates it for the sake of the purifier (*pavitra*) with the *aghora* mantra.

Then, having taken his thumb with his own hand, turned downward, and placed it [in the vessel]... while reciting either the *Mṛtyuñjaya* [mantra] or the *Īśa*, he should swirl it around and offer the *pośana* [water for rinsing]. Having given half of that to him, saying "Eat as you please," and upon being told "So be it," he too should eat. Then, facing north, the performer should remain seated and recite the *Īśa-mātṛ-stotra*.

At that time, one should not offer food after considering the lunar day (*tithi*). At the end of the meal, having taken a small amount of food and said, "Are you satisfied? and having received the response, "I am satisfied," one should cast the food toward the south upon the ground for him who has given his consent. Afterward, having cast [food] once each in front [of them],...

Having spread out [the offerings] upon a maṇḍala prepared with cow dung, having strewn sesame seeds with the left hand, and having offered a ball of food (*piṇḍa*) together with all the side-dishes and sesame seeds—placed on the ground with the right knee bent, facing south, and accompanied by the root mantra and ending with *svadhā* under the name of initiation—one should give the *piṇḍa*.

Having washed the palm of his hand with the vessel, he should sprinkle a stream [of water] all around the *piṇḍa* with that [water] while reciting the *Vāmadeva* mantra, saying "Namaḥ. Having placed that vessel face-down to the south, having worshipped it with fragrances and other offerings, having prostrated and asked for forgiveness, and having grasped it, he should offer sandalwood paste for the sake of the omen.

Having offered betel leaves and other items, one should give the twenty-four gifts according to one’s means. And [one should offer] that sacred thread (*pavitra*), a sacrificial cord (*yajñasūtra*), a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and rosaries; (line 9) a staff, a loincloth, ashes for the limbs, a sacrificial cloth, a parasol, a turban, an upper garment, clothing, and a golden ring. (line 10)

A golden vessel, ghee, oil, and other items for the meal; a bed, all types of grain, female slaves, and those who carry them away—these constitute the twenty-four gifts considered appropriate for *ekoddiṣṭa* rites. Then, having requested [the recipient], one should say: "With water in hand, [I offer] a lamp."

When he has said, "May it be so for you," and that water has been poured upon the ground, he should himself likewise say what was spoken by him [the recipient]: "May the givers of us increase, as well as the Śaivas; may our lineage be pure, free from disease, and may there be much to give for both of us."

He too, being pleased, should respond from that point; having offered the *arghya* vessel with the *sadyojāta* mantra and having set aside the vessel for the ancestors, he should turn it face-upward. After performing a circumambulation and pronouncing blessings, he should dismiss [the deities]. Having cast the *piṇḍa* into water and having bathed himself with water or ashes, he should eat together with his kinsmen. This is the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
Salutation to the illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti. May there be auspiciousness!
The Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Rite.

Thus, during the [observance] period... at the end of six months and at the end of a year, fifteen *ekoddiṣṭa* funeral rites (*śrāddhas*) must be performed. Beginning from the time of death until the end of the year, meals accompanied by water-jars (*sodakumbha*) must be provided; and until the end of the year, the *maraṇa-śrāddha* must be performed. Alternatively, beginning from the end of the year—

Until the end of the year, meals together with water-jars should be provided. Until the end of the year, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha must be performed. Or else—honoring his own station until the end of the year—having given the *aṣṭamāsika* śrāddha along with water-jars on the twelfth day or another auspicious day;

One should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite. Now, the second [procedure]: on the previous day, one should invite the *deśika* and others who possess the characteristics as previously described, having been consecrated according to the ritual for increasing [the merit]. For the sake of their satisfaction, one should accept the *deśika* and others for the purpose of the *viśvedevas*; in the absence of a practitioner (*sādhaka*), one should accept those established in the *samaya* vows.

Even for one who maintains only the householder’s stage of life (*gṛhastha*), he should take three [offerings]. In the absence of vessels possessing the characteristics as described, he should take a single vessel for the Viśvedevas and another for the ancestors (*pitṛs*). He should worship the Viśvedevas in one arm-pit and the ancestors in the other, distinguishing between the two by the division of the shoulder-blade.

Alternatively—if neither [of the two] is available—one [should worship] the Viśvedevas on the head and shoulders; one should worship the Pitṛs [on the remaining parts]. For the sake of the occasion, one should select one among the preceptor and others. Thus, having first performed the offering with due reflection, an invitation (*kṣaṇa*) must be made for the Viśvedevas in the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* Śrāddha, and an invitation must be made for the sake of the ancestors beginning with the father.
Having thus addressed [the deities], may there be auspiciousness.

On the following day, having performed their daily obligatory rites (*nityakṛtya*), both [the teacher and the disciple] should, in the afternoon, prepare two square areas the size of a *kuru* (a cubit), separated by one hand’s breadth and situated north-south, on the ground of the sacrificial enclosure smeared with cow dung;

having thus designated the space for the deities, and likewise having prepared the space facing east for the ancestors. Having performed their daily obligatory rites, they should proceed, honoring [the guests] with rising from their seats and other marks of respect, while holding the general water-offering (*sāmānyārghya*) in their hands, [worshipping] Dharma and the others within the square area.

Having placed the tips of the *darbha* grasses toward the east and sesame seeds between two circles, one should place *darbha* grasses with their tips pointing south within the two southern mandalas. Having washed the feet [of the deities] and worshipped them with white flowers using the *astra-mantra*, and having worshipped those in the northern mandala with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should offer the *arghya*. [Then] the two Viśvedevas [are to be worshipped] in the south.

Having established [the deities] within the square, and having offered a welcome-arghya with their respective names preceded by the *praṇava* and ending in *svāhā*, one should wash one’s feet with the Vāmadeva mantra. Having performed the *ācamana* in the northern square, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), one should establish Īśāna and the others in due order within the circular mandala in the south.

As before, having offered the *arghya* with sesame seeds ending in *svadhā*, he should wash his feet with clay using his left hand. Having sipped water (*ācamya*) on the northern mandala, and likewise for the *nimitta* [officiant], having first washed his feet and then sipped water; and from the *atithi* portion, having caused him to perform the washing of his feet right there where he stands.

Having sipped water and caused everyone to enter within, and having entered within himself as well, he should, starting from the southward direction, seat the Viśvedevas facing east on a purified ground, and the Pitṛs facing west on seats to the rear; then, having approached them with focused meditation, he should seat them on their respective seats with his left side [toward them].

Having performed the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa* with the [mantras] beginning with *sadyojāta*, having sprinkled the vessels for the special *arghya* offering with the *astra-mantra*, having filled them with pure water from the head [mantra], and having cast in water-lilies (*vān*), flowers, and sesame seeds; having applied fragrance with the *sadyojāta* mantra and having placed the *darbha*-strainer together with *durvā*, flowers, and unbroken rice grains using the *śikhā* mantra; having consecrated them with the *hṛdaya* mantra and protected them; having sprinkled the ritual substances; and having consecrated the fragrance, flowers, incense, lamp, cloth, and sacred thread in due order with the mantras beginning with the *hṛdaya* and ending with the *kavaca*; one should prepare the *nimitta-arghya* in the same manner as the *pavitra-arghya*.

Having requested, "I shall perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha," and being permitted by them with the words "Do so," he, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savyopavītī*), should worship the two Viśvedevas. There, having offered water for the feet and other honors to the two deities, he requests, "I invoke [you]," and being permitted with the words "Invoke [them]," he performs the invocation with: "Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra; obeisance to Ananta. Thus he invokes them.

If [the practitioner] is a *samāyin*, having invoked Nandimahākāla, he should perform the placement (*sthāpana*), the making present (*sannidhāna*), and the confinement (*sannirodhana*) with the left hand; for the sake of protection, he should scatter [offerings] in a clockwise direction toward the northeast; then, having offered the hem of the garment with the *aghora* mantra for the sake of making [the deity] present, he should collect it in that vessel and set it down.

With the knees resting on the ground, beginning from the feet and extending to the top of the head, one should step upon [the corpse] with the *aghora* mantra. Having smeared it with fragrant substances using the left hand, and having adorned it with flowers and other offerings, one should present incense and lamps with the *aghora* mantra, and sacred garments, the sacrificial thread (*upavīta*), and so forth with the *īśāna* mantra. Then, one should perform the ritual circumambulation by the right (*apasavya*).

Having given double-folded *darbha* grass with their tips pointing south as a seat for the ancestors using the *Sadyojāta* mantra, and having requested permission as before, he should—beginning from the east and ending with Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānti—if [the recipient] is a *samayin*, invoke [the deities] by their respective names preceded by the *praṇava* and the word "namas," and followed by "yu" and "rakta," while including Skanda, Caṇḍa, and Gaṇādhīśa.

Having performed the three rites beginning with placement (*sthāpanā*) with the left [hand], having provided protection (*rakṣā*) by means of sesame seeds in a counter-clockwise direction with the *Īśāna* mantra, and having offered [the oblation] with the *Aghora* mantra for the sake of presence (*sānnidhya*), one should step upon it with the *Īśāna* mantra while the knees are on the ground and the head is raised, using the nets of power (*śaktijāla*). Then, one should smear it with perfumes using the left [hand].

Having adorned [the deity] with flowers and other offerings, and having offered incense and lamps with the *aghora* mantra, one should present the purificatory cloth (*pavitra*), the garment, the sacred thread (*upavīta*), and so forth, with the *īśāna* mantra. Having worshipped them for this purpose as well, and having said, "May it be complete," and being told by them, "May it be complete," one should offer water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) into their hands.

Therefore, having placed water collected with *pavitra* grass into a vessel, and having set it down face-down in the south-western direction—the place of the ancestors—and having honored the guest who has arrived and offered him the general *arghya*, one should bring together food for the meal along with side dishes, boiled rice, gifts, and snacks; then, while circles are being traced with the hand before them:

Having given [the food] to the worthy recipients according to one’s means, and having consecrated the sacrificial ground with the fire through the five purificatory rites (*pañcasaṃskāra*) as is customary, he should request: "I shall perform the offering in this fire, which has become Śiva himself, after taking the first portion of all the cooked food and soaking it in ghee for the sake of purification by cooking. Having been granted permission with the words, "Do so," ... [he proceeds].

One should perform the *pitṛyajña* oblation: *oṃ mīśānāya patre svāhā*; *oṃ sadāśivāya pitāmahāya svāhā*; *oṃ śāntāya prapitāmahāya svāhā*; *oṃ śikhībhūtāyamukalaśivāya svāhā*. If [the sacrificer] is a *samayin*, having offered with these three [mantras], [one offers] to Skanda and the others on the paternal and maternal sides.

Having placed the remaining food—accompanied by ghee, molasses, and various side dishes—into the vessels according to the sequence beginning with the Viśvedevas, and having consecrated it for the sake of purification with the Aghora mantra, he should grasp the thumb of each person with his own hand and ensure that it is joined with the offered food.

Reciting either the *Mṛtyuñjaya* or the *Vāmadeva* [mantra], he should circumambulate Īśāna; having offered water with the *Īśāna* mantra, he should say to them, "Enjoy this! They too, restraining their speech, should eat. If the performer is present, standing facing north while reciting the *Īśāna* mantra, he should feed any guests who have arrived at that time with due consideration.

At the end of the meal, taking a little food and saying, "Are you satisfied? (l. 9), and having been told by them, "I am satisfied," he should cast that food on the ground and afterwards throw [the remainder] once. Having prepared a mandala there with cow dung, he should spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south using the *sadyas* mantra, and place sesame seeds upon it with the left hand. (l. 10)

Having placed three portions for the ancestors (*pitṛ*) and three for the mothers, using mantras ending with *svadhā*—beginning from the Earth and ending with Īśvara and Sadāśiva—and having offered one portion to the *nimitta*, [the officiant] should smear the shoulders and other parts of the initiates (*samayin*).

Having released the palm of the hand, he should either circumambulate counter-clockwise while reciting [the mantra], establish a stream [of water], worship them with perfumes and other offerings, ask for forgiveness, and dismiss them. Then, having performed the ritual rinsing of his own mouth (*ācamana*), he should give the rinsing of the mouth to them, beginning with the ancestors.

Having offered betel-leaf and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one’s means, preceded by the name of the deity, together with water from a sacred vessel (*satīrtha*), and having requested that [the offering] be inexhaustible, one should take some water and utter the word *svadhā*. The wise [responders] should say, "May it be so, *svadhā*. One should sprinkle that water on the ground and, as before, bow down, saying, "May the gods and the Rudras be satisfied."

Having first released the *pitṛpātra* with the *sadyas* mantra, one should turn it face upwards. Then, having released the *arghya* vessels, the *bandhuka* [relative] should bow to them and, following behind, dismiss them outside. One should give the middle *piṇḍa*, which is the portion for Rudra, to a woman for the sake of her son. The other *piṇḍas* should be cast into water for the sake of the *gotras* and the Brahmin. Then, having wiped away the remnants, washed one's feet, and performed the ritual sipping (*ācamana*), one should perform the *sakalīkaraṇa* and prepare the general *arghya*. Having smeared a mandala with cow-dung, one should place four pure vessels upon it.

Having cast into those [vessels] perfumed water, milk, sesame seeds, the tips of *darbha* grass, incense, and flowers; having worshipped Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta with their names joined by the dative case-ending (*caturthī*) and the initiation-name (*dīkṣānāman*) joined by the instrumental case-ending (*nimitta*), from the northeast (*uttara*) to the end of the west (*dikṣaṇa*); and having offered the *arghya*, incense, lamps, and so forth;

one should separate the water from the vessel of the *nimitta* into the [other] vessels starting from the northeast using the root mantra (*mūla*). Then, having discarded those vessels, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). If [the recipient] is a *samayin*: Skanda, Caṇḍa, Gaṇādhīśa, Pitṛ, Nandin, Mahākāla, and the two Vāruṇas.

In the worldly *āmaśrāddha*, [the deities are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa; the Pitṛs, the Viśvedevas, Yama, and Aruṇa. (l. 8) Regarding the domain of the half-āmaśrāddha, one should perform everything except the actual eating during the forenoon. Then, one should eat together with those possessed of wisdom.
(l. 9) Thus ends the procedure for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
Homage to the venerable Gurus.
May there be auspiciousness!

For the purification of any deficiency in conduct on the part of the initiate (*samayin*), one should offer a hundred, a thousand, or five hundred oblations with the root mantra. Having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should mentally renounce the principles (*tattva*) beginning with earth. One should then contemplate the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyātattva*) as the sacrificial site, which is of a pure nature.

Having visualized the seat as the *māyātattva* named Bindu, [the practitioner] should be engaged in the visualization of the body consisting of the digits (*kalā*) beginning with *Iṇḍikā*. Being engaged in the visualization of the external organs starting from *Vyāpinī* up to *Anāśrita*, and being engaged in the visualization of the internal organs starting from *Samanā* up to *Śakti*, with a mind one-pointed in meditation upon the Supreme Lord, having visualized Śiva whose nature is *unmanā*, and being endowed with the purification through the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*, he should unite [the self] with the Supreme Lord. At the time of the *pūrṇāhuti*, having visualized the two Suṣumṇā channels as the corners of the mouth (*sṛkka*), [he should offer it] into the circle of the mouth.

Having visualized the "lotus of the heart," one should visualize the openings of the throat, palate, and *payas* as being filled with streams of clarified butter (*ājya*). Having performed the visualization that these very streams of clarified butter consist of streams of nectar (*amṛta*), thereafter—the consciousness of the disciple, resembling a pure crystal gem—

Having established the disciple’s self within one’s own heart by means of the *recaka* breath-yoga for the seat and the *pūraka* breath for the fire of the *kuṇḍa*, and having brought about a state of equal flavor (*samarasībhāva*), one should effect the connection between the resonance (*nāda*) aroused from the root channel and one’s own [self] by means of the contemplation of their identity, through the upward movement of that [resonance].

Through the union of *nāda* and the *nāḍīs*, there is the third connection: the six *kalās* known as *a*, *u*, *m*, the *bindu*, and *nāda*, which correspond to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Anāhata; [these are located] in the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, the *bindu*, the aperture, and the station of the *dvādaśānta*.

Having brought about the dissolution of those syllables, this is the fourth [stage]. The power called *nāda* should flow upward through the middle of the *vṛścika* [channel] as far as *samanā*. This is the fifth, the *śakti-viṣuva*, having divided [the path] into three parts starting from *śakti* and ending at *samanā*, with a duration consisting of sixteen *truṭis*.

By the utterance up to the end of Śakti; the subsequent time [is reached] by the utterance up to the end of Vyāpinī through a duration consisting of seventeen *truṭis*. The further subsequent time [is reached] up to the end of Samanā through a duration of eighteen *truṭis*, from the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Thus, due to the cause of dissolution, there is the equinox (*viṣuva*) of time.

Then, because it brings about the manifestation of the Self in the state of Śiva—which is eternally present at the end of *unmanā*—one should instill the contemplation that "the reality is sevenfold. Having established that the Self pervades the entire creation, one should unite the disciple’s self with the state of Rudra within the supreme, partless (*niṣkala*) [state] joined with *unmanā*, for the sake of stability in the [spiritual] body (*puñja*). One should cast the *pūrṇāhuti*. For the sake of expiation, having offered eight oblations with the *astra-mantra*.
May there be auspiciousness!
